chapterTitle: Database Engine Internals: B-Trees and MVCC

parts.partTitle: Why Databases Don't Write to Disk Instantly

beats.headline: Why does a 4ms query suddenly take 4 seconds?
beats.subline: It is not your code. It is the storage engine fighting disk latency.
beats.narration: When your Spring Data query spikes from milliseconds to seconds, the bottleneck resides below the JVM. Databases do not write to disk on every commit; they use buffer pools and slotted pages to survive.

beats.title: The Mutation Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Memory is fast, Disk is slow
beats.narration: Updates hit the Buffer Pool and WAL buffer first. The engine marks pages as dirty in RAM, then flushes them to disk asynchronously. This prevents random disk I/O from killing your throughput.

beats.title: Slotted Page Anatomy
beats.caption: How rows sit inside a fixed 8KB block
beats.narration: Pages are fixed-size blocks. Tuples grow upward from the bottom, while the slot array grows downward from the header. This allows the engine to compact space without breaking external index pointers.

beats.title: B+ Trees vs LSM-Trees
beats.narration: Relational engines use B+ Trees for balanced lookups. LSM-Trees, used in distributed stores, trade read latency for massive write ingestion by using immutable files and background compaction.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Buffer pools avoid random disk writes
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Why InnoDB secondary indexes need two lookups →
beats.narration: That is the storage foundation. In Part 2, we compare Postgres heap tables versus InnoDB clustered indexes to see why secondary index lookups might be slower than expected.

parts.partTitle: Why InnoDB Secondary Indexes Need Two Lookups

beats.headline: Why does MySQL need two tree walks for one row?
beats.subline: It is the cost of clustered indexes. Here is how to fix it with covering indexes.
beats.narration: Why does a simple email lookup in MySQL often perform two B-Tree traversals? Because InnoDB stores the primary key in every secondary index. Let us break down the performance cost.

beats.title: InnoDB Bookmark Lookup
beats.subtitle: Secondary Index → Primary Key → Row Data
beats.narration: InnoDB secondary indexes do not point to disk offsets. They store the primary key. So you traverse the secondary tree to get the ID, then traverse the clustered tree to get the row.

beats.title: Optimizing with Covering Indexes

steps.explanation: Requires a second lookup to fetch the status column.
Includes status in the index leaf, avoiding the second lookup.

beats.narration: By using INCLUDE in your index, you store the status column right in the leaf page. The database satisfies the query entirely from the index, dropping heap fetches to zero.

beats.title: Postgres vs InnoDB
beats.narration: Postgres indexes store physical pointers. This makes lookups faster but makes updates expensive because every index must be updated if the row moves. InnoDB's clustered design favors sequential inserts.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Postgres indexes store physical ctid pointers
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Why WAL is the heartbeat of ACID durability →
beats.narration: Indexing is about trade-offs. In Part 3, we look at Write-Ahead Logging—the reason your data survives a power outage and how it keeps your database consistent.

beats.headline: Why does the database log before it writes?
beats.subline: It is the only way to guarantee ACID durability without destroying disk performance.
beats.narration: If a power outage hits, your RAM is wiped. How does the database ensure your committed transaction is not lost? It relies on the WAL—the Write-Ahead Log.

beats.title: The WAL Rule
beats.subtitle: Log first, flush later
beats.narration: The WAL rule is strict: no data page can flush to disk until its corresponding log record is safely persisted. This turns random page writes into fast, sequential log appends.

beats.title: ARIES Recovery Phases
beats.caption: How the engine restarts after a crash

lines.text: 1. Analysis: Scan WAL for dirty pages
2. Redo: Replay changes to match state

beats.narration: On restart, the engine performs ARIES recovery. It analyzes the log, redoes committed changes to restore the state, and undoes partial transactions to maintain atomicity.

beats.title: WAL vs Data Pages
beats.narration: WAL is your performance hero. By logging compact deltas sequentially, the database avoids the massive overhead of flushing entire pages to random disk locations on every commit.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: WAL rule: Log before data flush
Sequential I/O is faster than random
ARIES recovery restores state via log replay
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): MVCC—how readers and writers coexist →
beats.narration: WAL is the backbone of durability. In Part 4, we explore MVCC, the magic that lets your reporting queries run without blocking concurrent updates.

beats.headline: Why don't your reports block your transactions?
beats.subline: MVCC creates snapshots. Every transaction sees a private view of the world.
beats.narration: In older databases, a long report would lock tables and stop all updates. Modern engines use MVCC to keep multiple versions of a row, so readers and writers never clash.

beats.title: MVCC Versioning
beats.subtitle: Multiple versions, one snapshot
beats.narration: When Tx 102 updates a row, it creates a new version. Tx 101, holding an older snapshot, simply ignores the new version and continues reading the old one. No locks required.

beats.title: Inspecting Postgres MVCC
beats.caption: Watch tuple versioning in real-time

lines.text: SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, balance FROM accounts;

beats.narration: Postgres adds new tuples on update. The old tuple stays at (0,1) until VACUUM cleans it up. You can see the xmin transaction IDs changing as new versions are created.

beats.title: Postgres vs InnoDB MVCC
beats.narration: Postgres creates new heap tuples on update, requiring autovacuum to reclaim space. InnoDB updates in-place and uses undo logs to reconstruct older versions for concurrent readers.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
takeaways: InnoDB uses in-place updates + Undo logs
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 5): Avoiding Write Skew and Bloat →
beats.narration: MVCC is the key to high concurrency. In Part 5, we wrap up with production pitfalls like Write Skew and how to prevent table bloat from killing your performance.

beats.headline: Your database is bloating—and you do not know why.
beats.subline: Long-running transactions are the silent killers of database performance.
beats.narration: A single idle transaction can stop autovacuum, causing your table to bloat from gigabytes to tens of gigabytes. Here is how to diagnose and prevent the most common production disasters.

beats.title: The Bloat Cycle
beats.subtitle: Idle transactions pin the snapshot horizon
beats.narration: When a transaction stays open, the database cannot reclaim dead tuples. They pile up, forcing the engine to scan through gigabytes of garbage just to find a few live rows.

beats.title: Defensive Monitoring
beats.caption: Catch bloat before it kills performance

lines.text: SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS age FROM pg_stat_activity;

beats.narration: Set statement timeouts to kill idle transactions automatically. Monitor dead tuple counts and transaction age to ensure autovacuum has the room it needs to keep your tables lean.

beats.title: Write Skew Prevention
beats.narration: Repeatable Read does not prevent Write Skew. Use Serializable isolation or SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock your read set, and always implement a retry loop for serialization failures.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Monitor dead tuples and tx age
Use Serializable + retry for Write Skew
beats.narration: You have mastered database internals. Check out the roadmap for the full deep dive into transaction isolation and performance tuning. Keep building.
